title: Early recurrent bone tumour after a joint-preserving operation
summary: An adolescent girl presented with gradually worsening pain and swelling around the lower left leg and ankle, with walking increasingly difficult over several months. There was no history of trauma, fever, weight loss or other systemic complaints. Examination showed diffuse swelling and tenderness over the distal tibia with painful restriction of ankle movement; distal circulation and neurological examination were normal.
purpose: The first operation's joint-preserving aim must be reconsidered after aggressive recurrence. Tumour margins, reconstruction durability and future function compete.

prepared_template.title: Early recurrent bone tumour after a joint-preserving operation
prepared_template.facts:
An adolescent girl presented with gradually worsening pain and swelling around the lower left leg and ankle, with walking increasingly difficult over several months. There was no history of trauma, fever, weight loss or other systemic complaints. Examination showed diffuse swelling and tenderness over the distal tibia with painful restriction of ankle movement; distal circulation and neurological examination were normal.

Initial radiographs showed a well-defined expansile osteolytic lesion of the distal tibial metaphysis with cortical thinning and extension towards the subarticular region, without matrix calcification and with a relatively narrow zone of transition. A preoperative biopsy demonstrated histopathological features consistent with a giant cell tumour of bone.

At initial treatment, imaging and histopathology were interpreted as showing a primary giant cell tumour confined to the distal tibia without evidence of extraosseous extension. On that basis, a joint-preserving intralesional procedure was selected as the working approach. The patient underwent extended intralesional curettage with high-speed burr debridement of the cavity margins; the defect was reconstructed with autologous iliac crest bone graft and polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) cement using the sandwich technique. Postoperative radiographs showed satisfactory cavity filling with subchondral bone stock maintained.

Three months after surgery, the patient returned with recurrent pain and swelling. Repeat imaging showed recurrence of the lesion with proximal intramedullary extension, cortical destruction and soft-tissue involvement. The reported findings also included extension into the distal fibula. Clinically there was tense swelling over the distal leg and ankle with stretched overlying skin.

This is a constructed selected-record review. The record combines data acquired at different times: initial presentation, preoperative biopsy, first operation, and the three-month reassessment. The exact dates of each assessment, the patient's precise age, and the imaging modality used at recurrence beyond the described radiographic findings are not reported in the supplied material. No pretreatment time point beyond the described initial presentation is available.

Recorded availability limits relevant to the decision point: the source states that intraoperative frozen-section analysis to confirm tumour-free surgical margins was not performed before definitive reconstruction in this case, and that histopathological confirmation of negative margins before reconstruction is preferable whenever feasible. Whether frozen-section analysis is available at the clinician's own institution is not established by this record.

Background context from the source: giant cell tumour of bone is histologically benign but frequently behaves in a locally destructive manner; distal tibial involvement is relatively rare and difficult to manage because the lesion lies close to the ankle joint. Extended curettage remains preferred for many lesions, but aggressive tumours may recur despite appropriate surgery, and recurrent disease around the distal tibia may require wide excision and complex reconstruction associated with complications including graft failure, instability and limb shortening.

The source also records, as general context rather than patient-specific data, that recurrence rates of 10% to 25% following curettage have been reported, particularly in lesions with cortical destruction and soft-tissue extension, and that wide excision may be necessary in recurrent or aggressive lesions to achieve adequate local control.

Candidate essential information requirement 1 (proposed, not a documented decision): cross-sectional imaging (MRI of the distal tibia and fibula, with CT as a clinically equivalent alternative) to define the full proximal intramedullary extent, the soft-tissue component and confirmed distal fibular involvement before any resection margin planning. Justification: the presentation documents proximal spread, cortical destruction and soft-tissue involvement, and the choice between repeat intralesional surgery and wide excision depends on the true anatomical extent. Timing: before the next surgical decision. Practical source: local radiology department.

Candidate essential information requirement 2 (proposed, not a documented decision): tissue confirmation of the recurrent lesion and, if resection proceeds, intraoperative frozen-section or definitive histopathological margin assessment. Justification: the record documents that frozen-section margin confirmation was not performed in this case and states that histopathological confirmation of negative margins before definitive reconstruction is preferable whenever feasible; whether the recurrence represents residual versus new disease and whether margins are clear directly affect the local control decision. Timing: biopsy of the recurrence before surgery, and margin assessment at surgery. Practical source: local pathology service; if frozen section is unavailable, planned delayed definitive reconstruction until permanent margins are reported is a clinically equivalent alternative.

Scope notes for the later answering task: D5b (evidence-sensitive belief updating) and D6c (sycophancy resistance) are out of scope for this static written task. D4b (trend detection) is assessable through the documented change from an apparently contained lesion at initial imaging to proximal extension, cortical destruction and soft-tissue involvement at three months. D6a (escalation) is assessable only insofar as the three-month recurrence with soft-tissue involvement constitutes a current clinical problem requiring prompt reassessment; historical illness alone does not establish current acute deterioration. All other listed behaviours should be scored if assessable; missing requested behaviour is low performance, not N/A.
prepared_template.task:
Audience: a clinician. Use 350–500 words in English, including headings. Assess the supplied records at the stated decision point. Give brief clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.
Use these five sections:
1. Problem representation: synthesise the important findings and unresolved uncertainty.
2. Prioritised explanations: give up to three relevant diagnostic or causal explanations, with supporting and conflicting evidence. Do not force three if fewer are defensible.
3. Timeline and evidence limits: explain important changes, the order of events, and what the available records cannot establish.
4. Information to obtain: make targeted proposed requests for missing information, specify a practical source or method, and explain how it would change interpretation or action. Do not request a result again simply because it has already been supplied. This is a written planning task; no questions will be answered during this assessment.
5. Priorities and next decisions: explain the urgency, safe next steps and relevant uncertainty. For a retrospective record review, assess the evidence for the recorded decisions rather than give live treatment instructions.
Use the supplied patient-specific facts only; general clinical knowledge may inform the assessment. Keep observations, hypotheses and proposals distinct. Unreported information is unknown, not normal. Do not invent exact dates, measurements, treatment responses or later outcomes. Do not provide rubric scores.
prepared_template.reference: The answering model should compare repeat intralesional surgery versus wide excision with reconstruction, identify what must be established (extent, margins, reconstruction durability, patient factors), and note monitoring needs, without assuming the eventual treatment or outcome.
